title: December TV Calendar: All Major Premieres & Finales You Can Print Now!
body:
The entertainment calendar for December 2026 is finally here, and it arrives as a sleek, printable guide that maps out every major television premiere and finale across broadcast, cable and streaming platforms. Compiled by industry insiders, the calendar is designed to help viewers navigate a crowded month that promises a mix of high‑stakes drama, comedic experiments and the final bows of several beloved series. From the highly anticipated Netflix limited series “Collect & Praise” to the concluding episodes of network power‑houses, the schedule offers a clear snapshot of what will dominate living‑room conversations and social‑media buzz through the holiday season.

One of the standout entries on the calendar is Netflix’s six‑episode limited series “Collect & Praise.” The dark comedy follows a charismatic megachurch pastor, played by rising star Druski, whose relentless pursuit of wealth collides with the unpredictable antics of his deacon, portrayed by veteran comic Mike Epps. The series taps into the current cultural fascination with religious institutions as profit‑driven enterprises, blending satire with sharp social commentary. Early screenings suggest a tone that balances biting humor with moments of genuine pathos, positioning the show as a potential breakout hit that could redefine the limited‑series format for streaming services.

Broadcast networks are not being outshone, however. The calendar highlights the return of several flagship dramas that will air their season finales in the final weeks of December. ABC’s long‑running procedural “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” is set to conclude its 28th season with a two‑part episode that promises to tie together lingering story arcs while delivering the franchise’s trademark emotional weight. Meanwhile, CBS is set to wrap up the final season of “NCIS: Los Angeles” with a high‑octane finale that will see the team confronting a global cyber‑threat, a narrative choice that reflects the network’s effort to keep the series relevant in an era dominated by streaming‑first productions.

Cable and premium channels are also making strategic moves. HBO Max will debut the sophomore season of “The Midnight Syndicate,” a gritty crime anthology that has quickly become a cult favorite for its cinematic storytelling and rotating director roster. The network’s decision to slot the premiere in early December signals confidence that the series can capture audiences before the holiday binge‑watch surge. Similarly, Showtime is rolling out the finale of “The Last Frontier,” a gritty western drama that has earned critical acclaim for its nuanced portrayal of frontier life and its complex character studies.

Streaming platforms beyond Netflix are leveraging the calendar to maximize subscriber engagement. Disney+ is set to launch “Starship Academy,” an animated sci‑fi adventure aimed at families, timed to coincide with school vacations. Meanwhile, Amazon Prime Video will introduce “Echoes of the Past,” a historical thriller that intertwines present‑day investigations with flashbacks to World War II espionage, reflecting the platform’s growing investment in genre‑blending narratives. These releases illustrate a broader industry trend: the convergence of traditional broadcast scheduling with the on‑demand flexibility that streaming audiences now expect.

The printable calendar itself is more than a simple list; it includes QR codes that link directly to official trailers, episode guides and exclusive behind‑the‑scenes content, turning a static schedule into an interactive planning tool. By providing a tactile, shareable resource, the creators aim to foster communal viewing experiences in an age where solitary streaming often dominates. The calendar’s design also underscores the importance of strategic programming, as networks and services align their marquee events with key rating periods, holiday advertising cycles and cultural moments.

Looking ahead, December’s densely packed lineup suggests that 2027 will likely see even tighter competition for viewers’ attention, prompting networks to double down on cross‑platform promotion and event television. As the industry continues to experiment with limited series, genre hybrids and interactive content, tools like this calendar will become essential for both audiences and marketers seeking to cut through the noise. For now, the printable guide offers a roadmap to a month of television that promises to be as diverse as it is compelling, setting the stage for the next wave of storytelling innovations.
